result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.all_topological_sorts()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} List every topological ordering of a DAG. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L36971-L37055){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.all_topological_sorts(max_sorts=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![All topological sorts](/assets/graphs/all-topological-sorts.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node DAG flowing left to right: A and B both point to C, which points to D and E. A and B can come in either order, and so can D and E, while C is always third. The card lists all four orderings in lexicographic order, from A, B, C, D, E to B, A, C, E, D." width="100%"} A topological ordering lists the nodes so that every edge points forward: each node comes after everything it depends on. `get_topological_sort_order()` returns one such ordering; most DAGs have many, and this method enumerates them all. The number of orderings measures how much freedom a schedule has: a chain has exactly one, while tasks with no dependencies at all can run in any of `n!` orders. Use it to explore every valid schedule for a small set of tasks, to check whether a given sequence is valid, or to count the linear extensions of a partial order. Because the count grows factorially, `max_sorts=` can cap the result on larger graphs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_sorts]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Stop after this many orderings. If `None` (default), return them all. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Each topological ordering as a list of node IDs, in lexicographic order of node IDs. An empty graph has one (empty) ordering. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or contains a cycle, or `max_sorts=` is below 1. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Getting dressed: socks and underwear can go on in either order, but shoes need both, and trousers need underwear: ::: {#3944761a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["underwear", "socks", "trousers", "shoes"]) .add_edges([("underwear", "trousers"), ("trousers", "shoes"), ("socks", "shoes")]) ) label = graph.get_label_from_id [[label(n) for n in order] for order in graph.all_topological_sorts()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['underwear', 'socks', 'trousers', 'shoes'], ['underwear', 'trousers', 'socks', 'shoes'], ['socks', 'underwear', 'trousers', 'shoes']] ``` ::: ::: Four independent tasks can run in any order, so `max_sorts=` keeps the result small: ::: {#49cae49e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} free = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) len(free.all_topological_sorts()), len(free.all_topological_sorts(max_sorts=5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (24, 5) ``` ::: :::
